title: Dynamic Arrays
body:
An [[Array]] whose size is decided at **run time**, allocated on the heap with `new[]` and
reached through a [[Pointer]].

```c++
int n;
cin >> n;
int* scores = new int[n];    // legal; int scores[n] is not

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
	scores[i] = 0;

delete[] scores;             // brackets required
```

This is the direct answer to [[Static Allocation]]'s limitation: `int scores[n]` with `n` from
input is a [[Compile Errors|compile error]], because the size had to be known before the
program ran. `new int[n]` runs after `n` has a value, so there is no problem.

The pointer indexes exactly like an array, because `scores[i]` *is* `*(scores + i)`; the
subscript operator was pointer arithmetic all along. Everything else is the same too: indices
run 0 to `n-1`, and C++ still does not check bounds.

What you give up:

- You have to `delete[]` it, or it leaks. See [[new And delete]] and [[Variable Lifetime]].
- `sizeof` no longer tells you the length, it tells you the size of a pointer. Carry `n`
  yourself, usually alongside the pointer in a [[Structure]].
- It is still a **fixed** size once allocated. "Dynamic" means chosen at run time, not
  resizable. Growing it means allocating a bigger one, copying, and deleting the old.

That last point is the seam where this course stops and [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] starts: the
resize-and-copy strategy, doubling the capacity so the copies amortise, is what `vector`
actually does. Here you either size it once from input or reach for a [[Linked Structure]]
instead.
